strengths: Excellent algorithm-system co-design: The integration of causal distillation (DMD, Self-Forcing) with Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) eleganty breaks the sequential bottleneck of diffusion models across multiple GPUs.

Unprecedented long-horizon stability: Successfully demonstrates stable avatar generation for over 10,000 seconds without quality decay, color shifting, or identity drift, which is a major bottleneck in autoregressive diffusion rollouts.

Well-reasoned and thoroughly ablated algorithmic modifications: Strategies like History Corrupt (using noisy representations in KV cache), Adaptive Attention Sink (AAS), and Rolling RoPE are well-motivated and verified through complete ablations.

Strong quantitative and qualitative results: Live Avatar achieves 45.2 FPS (with a 1.21s TTFF) on 5x H800 GPUs using a massive 14B parameter model, vastly outperforming existing large-scale avatar methods in both speed and long-term consistency.
weaknesses: High compute/hardware requirements: Running the 14B model in real-time requires multiple high-end datacenter GPUs (e.g., 5x H800), which limits immediate accessibility for consumer-grade edge deployment.

Relies on a static-scene prior: The proposed long-horizon stability strategies (such as storing only noise in KV cache to propagate only motion, while anchoring identity to the sink frame) are tightly coupled with the portrait/avatar scenario. The method may not directly generalize to videos with highly dynamic camera shifts or dramatic background changes.

strengths: An elegant algorithm-system co-designed framework that successfully scales up audio-driven video diffusion to a massive 14-billion-parameter model (WanS2V) while enabling real-time streaming.

Novel algorithmic strategies to handle long-horizon drift: History Corrupt (storing noisy KV caches as a low-pass filter), Adaptive Attention Sink (aligning latent manifolds), and Rolling RoPE (preventing index-drift out-of-distribution issues).

Highly creative system-level design with Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP), which assigns fixed timesteps to individual GPUs, effectively transforming the sequential diffusion process into a spatial pipeline and drastically boosting throughput to 45 FPS.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation, including a long-horizon benchmark (GenBench), extremely long 10,000-second stress tests, a double-blind user study, and granular ablation studies.
weaknesses: High hardware barrier to entry: To achieve the reported real-time streaming performance (45 FPS), the system requires 5 expensive datacenter-grade GPUs (such as H800s) due to the timestep-to-device mapping of TPP.
The Time-to-First-Frame (TTFF) of 1.21 seconds, while practical for some streaming settings, remains slightly too slow for highly responsive, low-latency conversational agent applications.

The long-horizon stability strategies rely heavily on the static-scene prior of avatar interactions. If the background changes dynamically or the speaker exhibits significant translation/camera movement, the assumption of using a persistent static sink frame (AAS) may cause artifacts or visual inconsistencies.

strengths: A well-conceived algorithm-system co-design that effectively scales and optimizes a 14B parameter diffusion model for real-time video streaming.
Outstanding performance in long-duration generation, demonstrating stable, drift-free talking-head outputs up to 10,000 seconds, far exceeding previous state-of-the-art frameworks.

The Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) represents a clever hardware-aware parallelization strategy, allowing multiple GPUs to work concurrently across the denoising chain with minimal inter-device communication overhead.
Highly comprehensive evaluation, with extensive ablation studies, a standardized long-form benchmark (GenBench), and a user study validating both quantitative metrics and human preference.
weaknesses: High hardware requirements: The optimal setup to achieve 45 FPS requires 5 high-end H800 GPUs, which limits applicability for typical consumer-grade or budget setups, although some cost-effective alternatives (e.g., H20) are explored.

Assumption of static-scene priors: The proposed long-horizon stability mechanisms (History Corrupt and Adaptive Attention Sink) rely heavily on the subject and background remaining relatively static, potentially limiting generalization to scenarios with highly dynamic cameras or background elements.

High Time-to-First-Frame (TTFF): While the frame rate is fast once the pipeline is warm, the 1.21s TTFF (coupled with standard network transit) creates a ~3-second initial latency that could hinder fluid, turn-taking conversational virtual assistants.

strengths: A compelling algorithm-system co-design that enables a massive 14B parameter diffusion model to achieve real-time (20 FPS) streaming video generation.

The proposed Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism (RSFM)—incorporating Adaptive Attention Sink (AAS) and Rolling RoPE—is highly effective at mitigating identity drift, color shifts, and distribution drift over extremely long horizons (extending up to 10,000 seconds).

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) offers an innovative way to bypass the sequential denoising bottleneck of diffusion models by pipelining timesteps across multiple GPUs without requiring inter-GPU KV-cache transfer.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation, including a newly created GenBench (short and long subsets), clear ablation studies on both system speed and long-term visual quality components, and a double-blind user study.
weaknesses: High hardware requirements: Achieving 20 FPS requires 5x NVIDIA H800 GPUs, which limits the accessibility of the proposed system for average developers and consumer-grade applications.

Interactive latency bottleneck: While the throughput (FPS) is excellent, the Time-to-First-Frame (TTFF) is still around 2.89 seconds (as shown in Table 3). This multi-second delay before the avatar starts speaking could be a major drawback for highly responsive interactive conversational systems.

Slight degradation in dynamic details: Step distillation causes a small drop in dynamic lip-sync quality (Sync-C and Sync-D metrics) compared to the original teacher model (WanS2V), which is a common but notable trade-off of distribution matching distillation.
Limited analysis on the sensitivity of the 'History Corrupt' noise scale during the distillation phase.

strengths: Novel algorithm-system co-design that enables real-time streaming of a very large (14B) video diffusion model for talking avatar generation.
The proposed Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP) elegantly parallelizes the sequential denoising process across multiple GPUs by leveraging same-noise level KV caching.

The Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism (RSFM), including Adaptive Attention Sink and Rolling RoPE, successfully addresses the long-standing problem of identity drift and color accumulation in infinite-length video generation.
Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations, including a new long-video benchmark (GenBench) and an ablation study on system performance.
weaknesses: Extremely high hardware cost for practical deployment: requiring 5 x H800 GPUs to generate a single real-time stream (20 FPS) is prohibitively expensive for most commercial interactive applications.

Very high training complexity and cost: training the model requires approximately 500 GPU days on H800 GPUs, which significantly limits the reproducibility of the work for the broader academic community.

Potential risk of noise propagation: in TPP, denoising at step $t$ conditions on the historical KV cache at the same step $t$ (which is noisy). While the authors show empirical benefits, relying on noisy history might cause error propagation or visual artifacts when there are sudden changes in audio or motion dynamics.

Limited evaluation on fine-grained identity consistency: the metrics used (ASE, IQA) are general perceptual quality metrics, which may not fully capture subtle identity distortions over long horizons. A more focused user study or quantitative face-recognition-based identity consistency metric over long durations would make the evaluation more convincing.

strengths: Excellent algorithm-system co-design that effectively addresses the sequential bottleneck of diffusion models, enabling a massive 14B parameter model to achieve real-time performance (over 20 FPS) via Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism (TPP).

The proposed Rolling Sink Frame Mechanism (RSFM), which combines Adaptive Attention Sink (AAS) and Rolling RoPE, presents a highly effective and novel solution to the long-standing problem of identity drift and color artifacts in autoregressive generation. Demonstrating stable generation up to 10,000 seconds is exceptionally impressive.

Comprehensive evaluation on standard datasets and a newly introduced benchmark (GenBench), supported by thorough ablation studies and a double-blind user study that demonstrates strong alignment with human perception.
Highly detailed supplementary material containing pseudocode for all algorithms (Algorithms 1-4) and clear system timeline visualizations, greatly enhancing reproducibility.
weaknesses: High hardware requirements: The TPP inference pipeline relies on 5x H800 GPUs to achieve the real-time target, which limits the deployment of this method on edge devices or standard consumer-grade setups.

Initial latency (TTFF): While the steady-state throughput is excellent, the Time-To-First-Frame is still around 2.89 seconds. This initial lag could be a minor bottleneck for near-instantaneous interactive live applications.

Substantial training cost: The two-stage training strategy (Diffusion Forcing Pretraining and Self-Forcing DMD) requires a massive compute budget (500 GPU days on 128 H800 GPUs), making retraining or fine-tuning challenging for resource-constrained teams.

Potential risk of error propagation in AAS: Since the original reference image is replaced by the first generated frame as the persistent sink, any visual artifacts or unnatural facial expressions in the very first block might propagate indefinitely across the entire sequence.
